etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English laughter, laghter, laȝter, from Old English hleahtor (“laughter, jubilation, derision”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahtraz (“laughter”), from Proto-Indo-European *klek-, *kleg- (“to shout”). Cognate with German Gelächter (“laughter, hilarity, merriment”), Danish and Norwegian latter (“laughter”), Icelandic hlátur (“laughter”). More at laugh.

definitions.definition: The sound of laughing, produced by air so expelled; any similar sound.

quote.citation: 1899, Stephen Crane, chapter 1, in Twelve O'Clock:
quote.text: There was some laughter, and Roddle was left free to expand his ideas on the periodic visits of cowboys to the town.

definitions.definition: A movement (usually involuntary) of the muscles of the laughing face, particularly of the lips, and of the whole body, with a peculiar expression of the eyes, indicating merriment, satisfaction or derision, and usually attended by a sonorous and interrupted expulsion of air from the lungs.

quote.citation: 1646, Thomas Browne, Pseudodoxia Epidemica: […], London:  […]  T[homas] H[arper] for Edward Dod, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The act of laughter, which is caused by a sweet contraction of the muscles of the face, and a pleasant agitation of the vocal organs, is not merely, or totally within the jurisdiction of ourselves.

quote.citation: 1858 October 16, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “The Courtship of Miles Standish”, in The Courtship of Miles Standish, and Other Poems, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor and Fields, →OCLC:
quote.text: Archly the maiden smiled, and with eyes overrunning with laughter.
